summary:
The legislative branch was the Student Senate. It met at 5 p.m. every Tuesday, in Downing University Center 305 as of May 2010, Cravens Library 111 by 2012 while Downing was rebuilt, and the Senate Chamber on the second floor of the Downing Student Union from 2014. Quorum was a simple majority of members. Legislation took two readings, with the Legislative Research Committee reviewing every item in between and determining its constitutionality. A bill acted within the Senate's own jurisdiction; a resolution recommended university policy or stated the Senate's opinion.

The Senate held thirty-six seats across the period, redrawn twice. Until 2013 they were four senators from each of the four classes, two graduate senators, one Gatton Academy senator and seventeen at-large. Resolution 5-13-S, given its second reading on 26 February 2013 and referred to the spring ballot, cut the class seats to three each, created one senator for each of the six academic colleges, cut at-large seats to fifteen, added a seat for the president or delegated representative of each chartered regional affiliate, and wrote a Regional Affiliates article into the constitution. Resolution 1-13-F, passed 10 September 2013 and ratified in the fall election with 310 yes votes of 426 cast, created one Navitas or English as a Second Language international student senator and cut at-large seats to fourteen. Bill 1-17-S, passed 30-0 on 14 February 2017, replaced the affiliates with Regional Ambassadors nominated by each regional chancellor and confirmed by two thirds of the Senate and four of the seven executive officers, and added a South Campus liaison chosen by the president.

Attendance ran through the Judicial Council. The bylaws allowed a senator no more than three absences a semester unless the Council excused them; the Secretary of the Senate reported excessive absences to the Council and the Speaker, the member appeared to explain, and the Council decided within seven days. In November 2011 ten of thirty-six senators were called to review and two were dismissed after missing their hearings. From 17 March 2015 the bylaws required every vote to be by roll call or electronic ballot and the minutes posted within a week. Bill 4-17-S required each senator to keep one office hour a week for the rest of spring 2017.

SGA's posted legislation archive begins in fall 2011. It records 53 numbered items for 2011-12, 52 for 2012-13, 26 for 2013-14, 49 for 2014-15, 38 for 2015-16 and 63 for 2016-17. The 2013-14 figure is short: the posted spring 2014 list stops at Bill 7, while the Herald reported Bill 17-14-S passing on 1 May 2014. Spring 2017 alone reached Bill 29 and Resolution 10.

The Executive Cabinet could veto by majority vote and the Senate could override with two thirds. The posted archive records three vetoes in these years: a 2011 dance marathon bill, the 2014 smoke-free campus resolution and a 2017 resolution on the awards banquet. None was overridden, and the record shows an override vote only in the 2014 case.

structure.fact: Before the 2013 amendments the Senate was composed of four senior, four junior, four sophomore and four freshman class senators, two graduate senators, one Gatton Academy senator and seventeen at-large senators, thirty-six seats in all (Constitution 3.6).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, section 3.6

structure.fact: All but the four freshman senators and three at-large positions were elected in the spring; the four freshman senators, three at-large positions and the Gatton Academy senator were elected in the fall (Constitution 3.7). Vacancies after the fall elections were filled by presidential appointment with the approval of a majority of the Senate (3.8.1).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, sections 3.7-3.8

structure.fact: Senate members served one academic year. Those elected in the spring took office no later than two weeks after the fall term began; those elected in the fall took office no later than two weeks after the fall elections (Constitution 9.2, 9.3).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, section 9

structure.fact: The Speaker of the Senate was elected by the Senate serving in the spring semester for the next academic year, had to be at least a sophomore who had served one academic year as a senator, and had to post six office hours a week. The Secretary of the Senate was appointed by the Speaker and approved by the Senate (Constitution 3.2.4, 3.3.6, 3.3.8, 3.4.1).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, sections 3.2-3.4

structure.fact: Five standing committees existed under the constitution before 2016: Legislative Research, Student Affairs, Academic Affairs, Public Relations and Campus Improvements. Committee heads were appointed by the President and approved by a majority of the Senate (Constitution 5.1.2-5.6).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, section 5

structure.fact: A senator could be removed by impeachment: written endorsement of at least twenty percent of the Senate's membership to initiate, proceedings in special session presided over by the Chief Justice, no final vote sooner than fourteen days, and a two-thirds vote of the full membership of the Senate sitting as a judicial body (Constitution 3.10).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, section 3.10

structure.fact: Quorum for the consideration of business was a simple majority of the members of the Senate (Bylaws 4.2). The Senate met at 5 p.m. every Tuesday of the academic year unless it voted otherwise (Bylaws 3.1).
structure.src_label: Bylaws of WKU SGA, as adopted Fall 2005 and amended Spring 2013, sections 3.1 and 4.2

structure.fact: Senators were allowed no more than three absences per semester unless excused by the Judicial Council. The rule stood in the bylaws as proposed in Fall 2003 (Article III, Section 2) and survived unchanged into the bylaws as amended Spring 2013 (2.2).
structure.src_label: Bylaws of WKU SGA as proposed Fall 2003, Article III; and as amended Spring 2013, section 2.2

structure.fact: A senator with excessive absences was referred by the Speaker to the Judicial Council, had to appear before it to explain the absences, and the Council had to decide within seven days and notify all parties (Bylaws 2.5). The Secretary of the Senate notified the Council and the Speaker of excessive absences and notified the member of the pending judicial review within three Senate meetings (Constitution 3.4.8), and the Council took action in accordance with the attendance policy (Constitution 4.5.10).
structure.src_label: Bylaws as amended Spring 2013, section 2.5; Constitution as posted October 2012, sections 3.4.8 and 4.5.10

structure.fact: The Executive Cabinet held veto power over all legislation passed by the Senate, each officer casting one vote and a majority carrying the veto. The sponsoring committee had to receive a written explanation within forty-eight hours and the President had to give reasons at the next regular Senate meeting (Constitution 2.10.4).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, section 2.10.4

structure.fact: The Senate could override any Executive Cabinet veto by a two-thirds vote (Constitution 3.1.9). Under the bylaws the Cabinet had to vote to ratify or reject legislation within fourteen days of Senate passage, and legislation was considered approved if the Cabinet failed to act; an override took two thirds of the Senate present and voting (Bylaws 5.3).
structure.src_label: Constitution as posted October 2012, section 3.1.9; Bylaws as amended Spring 2013, section 5.3

structure.fact: All legislation went through two readings and was referred to the Legislative Research Committee after the first reading, with an author or designated representative required to attend and defend it within two weeks (Bylaws 5.3). The committee determined the constitutionality of all proposed legislation (Constitution 5.2.4).
structure.src_label: Bylaws as amended Spring 2013, section 5.3; Constitution as posted October 2012, section 5.2

structure.fact: Bylaw 6.1 restricted SGA funding: the association could allocate funds solely to students. This clause was the basis of the Judicial Council's December 2015 rulings against departmental funding bills.
structure.src_label: Bylaws of WKU SGA as amended Spring 2013, section 6.1

structure.fact: The Constitution could be amended only by a two-thirds vote of the full membership of the Senate followed by a referendum carried by a majority of the student body voting; the Judicial Council reviewed all constitutional amendments before the Senate's vote (Constitution 10.1, 4.5.9).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as posted October 2012, sections 4.5.9 and 10.1

structure.fact: Resolution 5-13-S, first read 19 February 2013 and given its second reading on 26 February 2013, cut each class delegation from four senators to three, created one senator for each academic college elected by students in that college for a total of six, and cut at-large senators from seventeen to fifteen. Total elected seats stayed at thirty-six.
structure.src_label: SGA Resolution 5-13-S, Resolution to Adopt Amendments to the Constitution and Bylaws (data/legislation/2012-13/r5-13-s.pdf)

structure.fact: Resolution 5-13-S added Constitution 3.6.9, seating the president or a delegated representative of each chartered regional affiliate as a senator, and created Article 6, Regional Affiliates, setting out chartering by a resolution of the Senate, transmission of regional enactments to the SGA president within forty-eight hours, Judicial Council review of any regional enactment on the request of any student, and a right of appeal to the Judicial Council for anyone impeached by a regional affiliate.
structure.src_label: SGA Resolution 5-13-S, marked-up Constitution Article 6 (data/legislation/2012-13/r5-13-s.pdf)

structure.fact: Resolution 5-13-S also cut the Organizational-Aid Board from ten members to at least six, changed the term of a Judicial Council justice from one academic year to the duration of their academic career, cut the Senate Secretary's posted office hours from five a week to two, and struck the bylaws article on the Parliamentarian and Sergeant-at-Arms.
structure.src_label: SGA Resolution 5-13-S, marked-up Constitution sections 3.4.9, 7.1.1 and 10.4 and Bylaws Article II (data/legislation/2012-13/r5-13-s.pdf)

structure.fact: Resolution 1-13-F, first read 27 August 2013 and given its second reading on 10 September 2013, added Constitution 3.6.6, one Navitas or English as a Second Language International student senator, and cut at-large senators from fifteen to fourteen. It argued the case on enrolment, citing 498 international students in fall 2003 against 766 in fall 2012.
structure.src_label: SGA Resolution 1-13-F, Resolution to Adopt an Amendment to the Constitution

structure.fact: Resolution 1-14-S, first read 4 February 2014 and given its second reading on 25 March 2014, raised the Judicial Council from five justices to seven, moved selection of the Chief Justice from presidential appointment to a majority vote of the Council with Senate approval, and created the office of Associate Chief Justice.
structure.src_label: SGA Resolution 1-14-S, Resolution to Adopt Amendments to the Constitution and Bylaws

structure.fact: By the constitution as amended in spring 2016 the Senate stood at three senators from each class, two graduate senators, one English as a Second Language International student senator, one Gatton Academy senator, one senator from each of the six academic colleges and fourteen at-large senators, plus the president or delegate of each chartered regional affiliate.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Constitution as amended Spring 2016, section 3.6

structure.fact: Bill 1-17-S, first read 7 February 2017 and passed 30-0 on 14 February 2017, rewrote Article 6. Regional affiliates that chartered their own constitutions were replaced by Regional Ambassadors nominated by their Regional Chancellor and approved by a two-thirds vote of the Senate and a four-of-seven vote of the Executive Council, removable by the same route, with one ambassador per campus and a South Campus liaison selected by the SGA president.
structure.src_label: SGA Bill 1-17-S, Bill to Amend the Constitution to reform regional campus representation (data/legislation/2016-17/bill_1-17-s.pdf)

structure.fact: Bills 16-16-F and 17-16-F, both first read 1 November 2016 and passed on 15 November 2016, made the Sustainability Committee a permanent committee at Constitution 5.8 and MyCampusToo a permanent committee at 5.7 under the name the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion.
structure.src_label: SGA Bills 16-16-F and 17-16-F (data/legislation/2016-17/bill-16-16-f.pdf, bill_17-16-f.pdf)

structure.fact: Bill 27-17-S, passed 27-0-1 on 4 April 2017, made SGA SAVES a permanent committee as the Committee Standing Against Violence and Ending Self-harm, charged with matters of mental health and sexual assault awareness.
structure.src_label: SGA Bill 27-17-S (data/legislation/2016-17/bill_27-17-s.pdf)

structure.fact: Bill 21-17-S, first read 21 March 2017 and passed 24-7-0 on 4 April 2017, replaced the 2.5 cumulative grade point average required of any elected or appointed SGA member in Constitution sections 2.2.1, 3.2.1 and 4.2.3 with 2.0, the standard for good academic standing at WKU.
structure.src_label: SGA Bill 21-17-S (data/legislation/2016-17/bill_21-17-s.pdf)

structure.fact: Committee heads remained presidential appointments subject to a majority vote of the Senate. Bill 25-17-S, which would have moved the appointment to the Speaker of the Senate, failed 15-13-0 on 4 April 2017.
structure.src_label: SGA Bill 25-17-S (data/legislation/2016-17/bill_25-17-s.pdf)

structure.fact: Senates were numbered. The senate of 2015-16 was the Fourteenth Senate, that of 2016-17 the Fifteenth Senate, and that of 2017-18 the Sixteenth Senate, as recorded in the opening line of each meeting's minutes.
structure.src_label: SGA Senate minutes, 13 September 2016 (data/documents/2016-17-senate-minutes-smm-9-13-16.pdf) and 12 September 2017 (data/documents/2017-18-senate-minutes-09-12-17.pdf)

structure.fact: The Fifteenth Senate held twenty-four numbered meetings between 30 August 2016 and 25 April 2017, its committees chaired by Amy Wyer then Stephen Mayer (Academic Affairs), Zach Jones (Campus Improvements), Brian Anderson (Legislative Research), Michael Shelton then Helen Vickrey then Andi Dahmer (MyCampusToo), Savannah Molyneaux (Sustainability), Emily Houston (Student Affairs), Alex Sergent then Morgan Wysong (Public Relations) and Francisco Serrano then Hizareth Linares (SGA SAVES).
structure.src_label: WKU SGA legislative minutes, 2016-17

structure.fact: SGA's posted legislation archive begins with Fall 2011 - Spring 2012 and lists 53 numbered items for that session, 52 for 2012-13 including one executive action, 26 for 2013-14, 49 for 2014-15, 38 for 2015-16 and 63 for 2016-17.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Legislation Archive (2011-2025)

structure.fact: Numbering per semester in the posted archive reached Bill 23 and Resolution 4 in fall 2011; Bill 21 and Resolution 6 in spring 2012; Bill 17 and Resolution 4 in fall 2012; Bill 21 and Resolution 9 in spring 2013; Bill 17 and Resolution 4 in fall 2013; Bill 16 and Resolution 14 in fall 2014; Bill 14 and Resolution 10 in spring 2015; Bill 12 and Resolution 9 in fall 2015; Bill 15 in spring 2016; Bill 24 and Resolution 4 in fall 2016; and Bill 29 and Resolution 10 in spring 2017.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Legislation Archive (2011-2025)

structure.fact: Resolution 4-12-F, first read 13 November 2012 and passed 27 November 2012, supported the reorganisation of the Associated Student Body at the Glasgow campus into the Glasgow Student Body Association so that it could become a regional affiliate of SGA.
structure.src_label: SGA Resolution 4-12-F

structure.fact: Resolution 1-15-F, first read 1 September 2015 and passed 8 September 2015, recognised the Elizabethtown/Ft. Knox Student Body Association as a regional affiliate. By autumn 2016 SGA's website listed two Student Body Associations, Elizabethtown-Fort Knox and Glasgow.
structure.src_label: SGA Resolution 1-15-F; WKU SGA Legislative Branch page, archived 11 October 2016

structure.fact: SGA's posted senate roster for 2015-16 named the Speaker and twenty senators; the roster posted in October 2016 named the Speaker and seventeen senators, against thirty-six constitutional seats.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Legislative Branch page, archived 19 September 2015 and 11 October 2016

unanswered:
Things I could not establish, and where the record is silent.

1. 2010-11 legislation. SGA's posted legislation archive begins with Fall 2011. No bill or resolution numbers, texts or vote records survive online for 2010-11, and none are held in data/legislation/. Everything the archive knows about that year's legislative output comes from Herald reports of individual meetings.

2. Total senate membership in 2010-11. The Herald of 11 February 2011 reported 50 SGA members and the April 2011 election filled 36 senate seats, which matches the constitution as posted in October 2012. I could not find a constitution snapshot dated inside 2010-11 to confirm the seat table was the same that year.

3. Whether the international student seat was ever filled. The Navitas/ESL seat was created by referendum in September 2013 and appears in the constitutions of 2016 and 2017, but no election result or roster I found names the senator who held it, in any year of this block.

4. When the seat's wording changed. Resolution 1-13-F wrote "Navitas or English as a Second Language International student senator"; the constitution as amended spring 2016 reads only "English as a Second Language International student senator." The legislation that made that change is not in the posted archive.

5. Owensboro. Cain Alvey told the Herald in March 2013 that the amendment guaranteed representation for regional campuses "such as Glasgow and Owensboro," but I found no chartering resolution for an Owensboro student body association. Only Glasgow (2012) and Elizabethtown/Ft. Knox (2015) appear as chartered affiliates, and the SGA site in autumn 2016 listed those two.

6. Override attempts. Only one override vote is documented, the failed attempt on the smoke-free campus resolution on 4 December 2014. For the 2011 Danceathon veto the archive table records the veto and nothing further; for Resolution 1-17-S the document says "veto not overturned," which does not tell us whether a vote was held.

7. Attendance records. SGA's website carried a "Senate/Committee Attendance" accountability page from at least 2012, and Bylaw 2.7 required minutes and votes to be posted from March 2015, but no archived snapshot I retrieved contains any actual attendance table. Beyond November 2011 I found no numbers for how many senators were referred to the Judicial Council in any semester.

8. Spring 2014 volume. The posted archive stops at Bill 7-14-S and Resolution 2-14-S, while the Herald records Bill 17-14-S and Resolution 6-14-S passing on 1 May 2014 and Resolution 3-14-S in February. The posted record for that semester is incomplete and I could not reconstruct the missing items.

9. Judicial Council minutes and opinions for these years are not online. The wku.edu judicial minutes directories begin with 2018-19. What the Council decided about absentees, other than through Herald reports and the Chief Justice's oral reports in senate minutes, is not recoverable from the sources I reached.

10. wkuherald.com is behind a Cloudflare challenge and returned 403 to every request in this run, by direct fetch and through WebFetch. Herald claims above come from articles already cited in data/years.json or from the WKU Archives index of the printed issues; I could not run new full-text searches of the paper.

summary:
The Associated Students kept a judicial body through the whole decade, under two names and at least four sizes. The 1971 Talisman described a seven-member Judicial Committee for 1970-71 that interpreted the constitution, heard appeals of all election disputes, ruled on student traffic violations and considered conduct questions referred by the Dean of Student Affairs. Its photograph caption named eight people and gave David Eyler as chairman. Senior listings in the same volume, and President John Lyne's own essay, called the body the Judicial Council.

Students approved a new Associated Students constitution on 10 December 1970 by 1,397 to 697, with 2,094 voting; the Herald listed strengthening the judicial system among its key issues, and the document went on to the administration and the Board of Regents. Congress passed a further revision 23 to 0 on 2 March 1972, twenty-two votes being needed to pass it, and students ratified it 157 to 16 across 29 and 30 March 1972. The Herald reported that the judicial branch had been revised to clarify judicial processes on campus and that the constitution took effect when officers were installed on 27 April 1972.

Members were appointed, not elected. In April 1972 the Herald described a five-member council made up of people appointed by president Linda Jones or former president John Lyne, chaired by John Knight. That council ruled Kim Weaver ineligible to run for president at 7 p.m. on 5 April 1972; the nine-member Student Affairs Board overruled it the next day, holding Weaver had not had a fair hearing. On 13 April five of the council's eight members disqualified themselves and it declined to hear Bob Hatfield's election appeal. The 1973 Talisman put the council at ten under Don Carter, hearing appeals on parking tickets, dorm campusing and election violations; residence-hall boards sent it about 100 conduct cases in 1971-72.

Marc Levy's charge that treasurer David Payne had spent before the budget was approved was heard on 23 October 1975 and decided for Payne. Congress opened impeachment proceedings against the council's own chairman, Gerard Faulk, on 16 March 1976, six members moving where the constitution required five. Hearings ran three weeks. On 6 April 1976 the roll call was none for removal, 12 against and 16 abstaining, with 28 members present, short of the three-fourths of full membership removal required. Faulk chaired the seven-member judicial branch listed for 1976-77. The council voted 6 to 1 on 5 October 1976 to drop the Maranatha payment case, and in April 1978 it denied Ed Johnson's appeal against Steve Thornton's election. In September 1978 Bob Moore's appointment as chairman lapsed because the constitution barred staff from the council.

structure.fact: The 1971 Talisman described the Judicial Committee as consisting of seven student members, and said it interpreted the A.S. Constitution, heard appeals of all election disputes, ruled on student traffic violations, and considered questions of student conduct referred to it by the Dean of Student Affairs.
structure.src_label: 1971 Talisman, Associated Students, p. 68

structure.fact: The Judicial Committee photograph caption in the same volume named eight people: Sam DeShazer, Jeanne Jackson, Michael E. Freville (vice-chairman), Linda Jones (secretary), Brad Coffman, Mark Barber, Pat Riley and David Eyler (chairman). The count of eight in the caption does not match the seven stated in the text.
structure.src_label: 1971 Talisman, Associated Students, p. 68

structure.fact: A separate Rules and Elections Committee set all election laws, decided disputes arising from elections, and considered and reported on proposed amendments to the constitution. Its members were Phil Myers, Rita Highbaugh, Cathy Ashabraner, Alice Thomason, Gary Whittington, Ken Bowman, Rick McClain, Earl Bush and Ed McGee.
structure.src_label: 1971 Talisman, Associated Students, p. 68

structure.fact: Five-member residence hall hearing boards heard about 100 disciplinary cases in their first year, 1971-72. The system allowed appeals first through the Associated Students Judicial Council and finally through the Office of Student Affairs.
structure.src_label: 1972 Talisman, Student Affairs, p. 117

structure.fact: The Herald described the Judicial Council in April 1972 as a five-member body consisting of persons appointed by the sitting ASG president, Linda Jones, or by former president John Lyne. John Knight was its chairman.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 51:47, 7 Apr 1972

structure.fact: One week later the Herald reported that five of the eight members of the Judicial Council disqualified themselves at a pre-hearing conference. The membership figure of eight does not match the five reported on 7 April 1972.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 51:49, 14 Apr 1972

structure.fact: A nine-member Student Affairs Board sat above the Judicial Council and heard Kim Weaver's appeal on 6 April 1972. Four of its members were from ASG (Linda Jones, Reginald Glass, John Knight and Albert Stith) and five were university staff (Dean Charles Keown, Mrs. Anne Murray, Dean Jack Sagabiel, Dr. Jack Thacker and Dr. William Cunningham). Keown presided.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 51:47, 7 Apr 1972

structure.fact: A new Associated Students constitution was approved by the student body on 10 December 1970 by 1,397 votes to 697, on a turnout of 2,094 students, about 23 per cent of those eligible. The Herald reported that key issues in the document were a student bill of rights and strengthening the judicial system, and that it would go next to the University administration and ultimately to the Board of Regents.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 50:27, 11 Dec 1970

structure.fact: Congress voted 23 to 0 on 2 March 1972 to accept the proposed constitution; twenty-two votes in favour were needed for passage. The Herald said the vote culminated nearly a year and a half of deliberations by the administration and the Associated Students, and that the document would go to the administration and then to the student body for ratification.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 51:41, 3 Mar 1972

structure.fact: Students ratified the revised constitution 157 to 16 in a two-day referendum on 29 and 30 March 1972, with fewer than two per cent of Western's 10,133 students voting; a simple majority was required. The Herald reported that the judicial branch of the constitution had been revised to clarify the judicial processes on campus, and that the constitution became effective immediately following the installation of new ASG officers, scheduled for 27 April 1972.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 51:45, 31 Mar 1972

structure.fact: The 1973 Talisman described a ten-member Judicial Council led by Don Carter that heard student appeals on parking tickets, dorm campusing, election violations and other areas, and served as the deciding court for appeals of campus rule violations.
structure.src_label: 1973 Talisman, Associated Student Government

structure.fact: The 1974 Talisman named Robert Deboe, of Alpha Phi Alpha, as a member of the Judicial Council. This is the only naming of a Judicial Council member found for 1973-74.
structure.src_label: 1974 Talisman, Greeks, p. 254

structure.fact: The ASG constitution required at least five members of congress to initiate impeachment proceedings. Six of the 43 congress members present voted to endorse impeachment on 16 March 1976.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 51:47, 19 Mar 1976

structure.fact: Removal from office required the approval of three-fourths of the full membership of congress, according to the constitution. Discussion at the 23 March 1976 hearing ran past a 30-minute limit set by President Steve Henry.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 51:49, 26 Mar 1976

structure.fact: The Herald reported that Gerard Faulk would conclude a two-year term in the office of Judicial Council chairman during the 1976-77 ASG session.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 51:53, 9 Apr 1976

structure.fact: Charges brought before the Judicial Council on 23 October 1975 by Marc Levy and John Butchko rested on Article II, Section 3-D, point 3 of the ASG constitution, which stated that the treasurer shall spend funds as authorized by congress. Levy asked the council to rule that any expenditure made before 14 October 1975, the date ASG approved its budget, was illegal.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 51:17, 24 Oct 1975

structure.fact: An ASG organization chart for 1976-77 lists a Judicial Branch of seven: Gerard Faulk as chairman with Charlotte Antoine, Joe Phillips, Ed Mitchell, Nancy Holman, Patricia Cook and Megan Lake, plus three alternates, Teri Sell, Sue Ellen Young and Jim Matthews.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Records, SGA Organization Chart, 1976-77

structure.fact: A vote on a proposed constitutional amendment could not be taken at the 5 October 1976 congress meeting because two-thirds of congress were not present. The Herald noted the amendment had been on the floor three times.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 52:13, 8 Oct 1976

structure.fact: A set of four proposed constitutional and by-law amendments held in the SGA records is annotated with its outcomes: a precinct representation amendment failed, an Academic Council attendance amendment was marked DECLARED UNCONSTITUTIONAL, an attendance appeal amendment passed, and a roll-call votes amendment authored by Bob Moore failed. The document does not name the body that declared the attendance amendment unconstitutional.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Records, Proposed Constitutional Amendments, 1976

structure.fact: The attendance appeal amendment that passed provided that any congress member absent from more than six meetings must appear before congress to show cause why they should not be removed, after which congress votes on removal; a member who does not show cause at the first regularly scheduled meeting after being contacted is removed. Tim Leigh was its author and Pam Keown its sponsor.
structure.src_label: WKU SGA Records, Proposed Constitutional Amendments, 1976

structure.fact: The 1978 Talisman describes the appeal route in the spring 1978 presidential election: the protest was first rejected by ASG's rules and elections committee, which ran ASG elections, and then rejected by ASG's judicial council, which was the losing candidate's last source of appeal.
structure.src_label: 1978 Talisman, ASG, p. 35

structure.fact: The council had seven members in 1978. Its chairman was appointed by the ASG president, discussed with the executive council and brought up for approval at an ASG meeting.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 54:5, 7 Sep 1978

structure.fact: ASG's constitution said that a member of the judicial council shall not be a faculty or staff member. The Herald reported that the qualifications for membership were printed in the constitution.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 54:5, 7 Sep 1978

structure.fact: ASG had made constitutional changes annually since 1974, and the revised constitution approved on 28 November 1978 was the first to be presented to students for ratification. It changed congressional representation so that the 24 elected representatives could live on or off campus, replacing 10 off-campus and 14 on-campus seats, and added two graduate congress members from the graduate college's council and one voting member and one alternate from each college.
structure.src_label: College Heights Herald 54:28, 30 Nov 1978

unanswered:
Things I could not establish, stated plainly.

1. The constitutional text itself. No 1970s ASG constitution survives in the local repository or in the TopSCHOLAR SGA collection. That collection holds only the 1966 constitution, an 1986 constitution with amendments, 1994 bylaws and 2001-2002 constitutions. Everything reported here about what the constitution gave the Judicial Council comes from newspaper and yearbook descriptions of it, or from articles quoted in reports of particular cases (Article 2, Section 2, Part A-4 on candidate residency; Article II, Section 3-D, point 3 on the treasurer). I could not read the judicial article of any 1970s constitution.

2. How ordinary members were chosen. The Herald of 7 April 1972 says the council consisted of persons appointed by the sitting or a former ASG president. For 1976 and 1978 the record establishes only how the chairman was chosen: appointed by the president, discussed with the executive council, brought to congress for approval. Whether the other six or nine members went through the same approval, and what terms they served, is not established. The one term-length statement found is the Herald's remark that Faulk would conclude a two-year term as chairman.

3. Seat counts conflict and I have not reconciled them. Seven (1970-71 text) against eight (1970-71 caption); five (Herald, 7 April 1972) against eight (Herald, 14 April 1972); ten (1973 Talisman); seven plus three alternates (1976-77 chart); seven (Herald, September 1978). Each is reported above with its own date and source. I have no source that explains the changes.

4. The name. The 1971 Talisman calls the body the Judicial Committee in its organisation pages and the Judicial Council in its senior listings and in President Lyne's essay. I could not establish which was the constitutional name in 1970-71, or when the name settled.

5. Whether an ASG judicial body existed before 1970-71. A Herald index line for 14 November 1968 reads 'Judicial Council to Hear More Disciplinary Cases', but nothing in it ties that body to Associated Students rather than to the university's own student discipline machinery. I did not open the issue. The archive should not treat it as an ASG appearance without checking.

6. Chairs for several years. Known: David Eyler, 1970-71 (as Judicial Committee chairman); John Knight, April 1972; Don Carter, 1972-73; Gerard Faulk, 1975-76 and 1976-77. Unknown: 1973-74, 1974-75, 1977-78, and who replaced Bob Moore in 1978-79. Full membership is known only for 1970-71 and 1976-77.

7. The outcome of the Levy v Payne case is carried by the 1976 Talisman alone. The Herald reported the 23 October 1975 hearing and its adjournment; no Herald report of the decision appears anywhere in the complete index for October 1975 to March 1976.

8. Who declared the 1976-77 Academic Council attendance amendment unconstitutional. The SGA document is stamped DECLARED UNCONSTITUTIONAL and names no body. It is plausible but unproven that the Judicial Council did it, and I have not written it that way.

9. Continuation text lost to bad scans. The Herald issues from 1970 to 1972 and the April 1978 issues carry no usable machine-readable text; I read those pages as page images instead. The back-page continuation of the 7 April 1972 story names the Judicial Council members present at the Weaver hearing, and the continuation of the 7 September 1978 Moore story carries Thornton's remaining comments; I could not locate either continuation block in the scans within this run.

10. 1979-80 is silent. The complete Herald index carries no judicial item for the 1979-80 academic year, and none of the SGA documents for the period mention the council. I found nothing, which is not the same as nothing having happened. The March 1978 organization charts held in the SGA records list executive and legislative branches only and do not show a judicial branch at all.

Note on method: digitalcommons.wku.edu returned an AWS WAF JavaScript challenge on every viewcontent.cgi request, so no PDF could be downloaded from it directly. Landing pages served normally at one request every three seconds. The Herald and SGA PDFs used here were retrieved from Wayback Machine captures of those same TopSCHOLAR URLs; the citations point at the TopSCHOLAR originals.

summary:
The Associated Students of Western Kentucky University began as a document. A sixteen-member organizational committee, drawn from the class presidents and from the residence halls, departmental clubs, honor and professional groups and the Interfraternity and Panhellenic councils, met from November 1965 on a plan written by Dean of Students Charles Keown. President Kelly Thompson approved the finished constitution on 1 April 1966. The Herald printed it in full on 7 April. Students ratified it in a four-day vote, 1,812 to 726 on 2,538 ballots counted from the dormitories and from Thursday and Friday polling.

That constitution created four campus-wide executive officers, a Student Congress of twenty-five representative seats, a Judicial Council of seven appointed members, and three constitutional committees: Rules and Elections, Finance, and Student Activities. Seats were distributed by group, three to each of the four class councils, two each to the Interfraternity and Panhellenic councils, the men's and women's residence halls and the campus at large, and one each to the professional and honor groups, the departmental clubs and the general clubs. Terms ran one calendar year from the second week of May. Congress had to have two-thirds of its total membership present to transact business, and could expel a member by three-fourths secret ballot ten days after five members endorsed proceedings. Amendment took two-thirds of the full Congress, then a majority of students voting at a regular election, then the University's approval. The first Congress, elected in May 1966, seated twenty-five people: four officers and twenty-one representatives, with the freshman seats empty.

Congress reopened the text almost at once and never closed it. On 13 February 1969 it voted, 18 to 1 by the Herald's count, to create a revision committee of up to ten members. Four changes went to students in voting that closed on 1 May 1970; a quorum question went on the October 1970 ballot. A wholly new constitution carried a referendum on 10 December 1970, 1,397 to 697, after the Rules and Elections Committee refused to run the vote; it went to the administration and the record says no more about it. Congress approved a further draft on 3 March 1972, and students ratified it 157 to 16 in a two-day referendum on 29 and 30 March, on a turnout below two per cent of 10,133 students. Effective at the installation of officers on 27 April 1972, it renamed the body the Associated Student Government, split the vice presidency into administrative and activities posts, replaced the club, Greek and residence-hall seats with ten representatives-at-large and two from each academic college, and rewrote the judicial article.

Revision continued. Bill 2 created a revision committee in September 1976 and Bill 11 sent its work to a student referendum in April 1977; Congress approved a revised constitution on 30 November 1978 and passed amendments in February 1979; the 1983 revisions went on the April election ballot. By 1986 the accumulated text survived as a typed constitution of five executive officers, a Congress of class officers and college, on-campus, off-campus, at-large and freshman representatives, and a Judicial Council of seven with three alternates, bound with a separate sheet of further amendments.

structure.fact: The committee that drafted the constitution had sixteen places: the four class presidents, the sophomore and freshman vice presidents, a second senior and a second junior, and one representative each from the women's and men's residence halls, departmental clubs, general college clubs, professional and honor groups, the Interfraternity Council, the Panhellenic Council, and married students (that last seat unfilled). Dean of Students Charles Keown named them to President Kelly Thompson on 13 November 1965; the group met Tuesdays from 7 to 10 p.m.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Proposed Western Student Organization, Charles Keown, 13 and 16 Nov 1965

structure.fact: Keown's own draft, sent to Thompson on 16 November 1965, proposed a different body: a Student Association with an Assembly of 33 (four officers, three at-large representatives and two from each of thirteen groups), an Executive Council of seven, and a Judicial Committee of five. The adopted 1966 constitution used a Congress of twenty-five representative seats and a Judicial Council of seven.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Proposed Western Student Organization, proposed structure, 16 Nov 1965

structure.fact: The constitution of the Associated Students was printed in full in the College Heights Herald of 7 April 1966, page 8, under fourteen articles: Name and Membership, Executive, Legislative, Judicial, Constitutional Committees, Student Affairs Board, Advisor, Budget, Term of Office, Vacancies, Impeachment and Recall, Bylaws, Amendments, Ratification.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Herald, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article I made every full-time registered undergraduate a member of the Associated Students with equal voting rights, and divided the organisation into an Executive Branch, a Legislative Branch, committees, and a Student Affairs Board.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article I, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article II created four executive officers elected campus-wide: president, vice president, secretary and treasurer. A presidential candidate needed 45 semester hours of credit at a 2.25 grade point average, good standing, and two regular semesters in attendance; secretary and treasurer candidates needed 15 hours at 2.25. The president was a non-voting member of Congress except to break a tie; the other three officers voted.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article II, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article II, Section 6 created an Executive Council of seven: the four officers plus three representatives elected by and from Congress. It carried out Congress's policies, processed applications for recognition from student organisations other than Greek social fraternities, and gave the budget preliminary approval.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article II, Section 6, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article III, Section 4 listed twenty-five representative seats in Congress: three from each of the Senior, Junior, Sophomore and Freshman councils (president, vice president and one representative at large); one each from professional and honor groups, departmental clubs and general clubs; two each from the Interfraternity Council, the Panhellenic Council, the men's residence halls, the women's residence halls, and the campus at large.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article III, Section 4, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article III, Section 7 required two-thirds of Congress's total membership to be present for the consideration of business, and let Congress delegate executive power to the Executive Council for fixed periods by a three-fourths vote. Section 5 set representative qualifications at full-time undergraduate standing, a 2.0 average, and one semester in attendance except for freshmen, with 25, 55 and 85 hours for sophomore, junior and senior class representatives.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article III, Sections 5 and 7, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article IV created a Judicial Council of seven students appointed by the Executive Council and approved by Congress. Three took two-year terms and four took one-year terms; they took office no later than the second Thursday after fall registration and elected their own chairman and vice chairman. Members had to be juniors or seniors with a 2.25 average, and could not sit in Congress or have run for executive office that year.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article IV, Sections 1-3, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: The 1966 Judicial Council's listed powers included interpreting the constitution and bylaws on request, acting as a review board for contested enactments of Congress, hearing election disputes, passing on contested candidate qualifications, hearing student traffic violation and student conduct cases referred by the Dean of Students, and disciplining student organisations by censure, probation or suspension of recognition.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article IV, Section 4, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article V created three constitutional committees, Rules and Elections, Finance and Student Activities, each of five members, at least two of them seniors. Article VI created a nine-member Student Affairs Board: the Dean of Students as chairman, the Assistant Dean of Students, the Dean of Women, two faculty members named by the University president, the president and vice president of the Associated Students, the chairman of the Judicial Council, and one member of the Executive Council.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Articles V and VI, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article IX set the term: officers and all members of Congress took up their duties in the second week of May and served one calendar year. Article X filled vacancies by presidential appointment subject to Congress's approval. Article VII made the Dean of Students the advisor.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Articles VII, IX and X, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article XI let Congress remove any of its members for just cause by a three-fourths vote taken by secret ballot, acting as a judicial body. Proceedings needed the endorsement of at least five members, and no final vote could be called until ten days after they were instituted. An expelled representative could be readmitted by petition and a three-fourths vote.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Article XI, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: Article XII gave Congress its bylaws by a two-thirds vote and required that all election laws and regulations be in the bylaws. Article XIII allowed amendment by a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress followed by ratification at a regular election by a majority of the student body voting, with all changes subject to University approval. Article XIV made the constitution effective on University approval and a majority vote of students voting.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students, Articles XII-XIV, 7 Apr 1966

structure.fact: The ratification tally sheet held by WKU Archives breaks the 1966 vote down by polling place: yes 1,369 in the dormitories, 322 Thursday and 121 Friday, total 1,812; no 411 in the dormitories, 207 Thursday and 108 Friday, total 726. The sheet boxes 2,538 as the total vote.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Associated Student Government Constitution Ratification tally, May 1966

structure.fact: The roster of the first Congress, elected in May 1966, names twenty-five people: president Jim Haynes, vice president James E. Fox, secretary Carmen Ann Willoughby, treasurer Larry S. Heishman, and twenty-one representatives. No freshman council seats are listed and only one of the two women's residence hall seats is filled. Three representatives are marked as members of the Executive Council: David Arvin, Forrest Lanning and Marshall Peace.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Congress of Associated Students roster, 1966

structure.fact: The spring 1968 ballot put a constitutional amendment to students beside the cheerleader vote and a fee referendum. It would have required a candidate for treasurer to be an accounting or business major or minor with at least six credit hours of accounting including the current semester. The same ballot asked students to approve a $1.50 per semester registration fee increase allocated to the Associated Students for entertainment.
structure.src_label: UA3/3/1 Student Election Ballot, April 1968

structure.fact: Congress recorded absences by roll call. The minutes of 13 February 1969 open with the roll and name the two members absent.
structure.src_label: SGA Meeting Minutes, 13 Feb 1969

structure.fact: The constitution ratified on 10 December 1970 was described by the Herald as centring on a student code of rights and a strengthened judicial system, and as calling for a second vice president to handle entertainment, a restructured Congress and more financial autonomy. The document was to be sent to the University administration and then to the Board of Regents.
structure.src_label: Herald 50:27, 11 Dec 1970

structure.fact: The constitution ratified on 29 and 30 March 1972 changed the organisation's name from Associated Students to Associated Student Government. Years 1972-73 onward in data/years.json still carry the org label "Associated Students".
structure.src_label: Herald 51:45, 31 Mar 1972

structure.fact: The 1972 constitution created two vice presidencies where one had existed. The administrative vice president deputised for the president, coordinated all committees and assisted the president; the activities and programs vice president handled publicity and coordinated social and cultural activities.
structure.src_label: Herald 51:45, 31 Mar 1972

structure.fact: The 1972 constitution rebuilt Congress on ten representatives-at-large plus two representatives-at-large from each academic college, and removed the seats held by the Interfraternity Council, the Panhellenic Council, the residence halls, the general clubs and the professional and honor groups. It took effect immediately after the installation of the new officers, set for 27 April 1972, and the Herald called it the culmination of eighteen months of deliberation by two bodies of Congress.
structure.src_label: Herald 51:45, 31 Mar 1972

structure.fact: The organisation chart for 1976-77 shows the three branches as the 1972 constitution left them: an executive of president, administrative vice president, activities vice president, treasurer and secretary; a Judicial Branch of seven members and three alternates under chairman Gerard Faulk; and a legislative branch of eight class officers, college representatives, ten representatives-at-large and twelve Academic Council representatives. The same chart lists eight dismissals, three resignations and six appointments during the year.
structure.src_label: SGA Organization Chart, 1976-77

structure.fact: Two resolutions sought a new executive office after the Board of Regents transferred concerts and lectures to the University Center Board in March 1979. Resolution 79-18, dated 26 February 1980, supported amending the constitution to include a Vice President of Public Affairs; Resolution 80-14, dated 21 October 1980, again proposed creating the post.
structure.src_label: SGA Resolutions 79-18 and 80-14

structure.fact: Congress abolished its own Finance Committee by Bill 85-1-F on 17 September 1985, created a Financial Advisory Council by Bill 85-2-F on 1 October 1985, and wrote the council into the bylaws by Bill 86-3-S on 28 January 1986. The dates in data/years.json for the first and third of these (24 September 1985 and 2 April 1986) do not match the dates TopSCHOLAR gives.
structure.src_label: SGA Bills 85-1-F, 85-2-F and 86-3-S

structure.fact: The typed constitution TopSCHOLAR holds as the 1986 consolidation lists five executive officers elected campus-wide: President, Administrative Vice-President, Public Relations Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer. Candidates needed a 2.35 average, two full semesters at Western and 30 hours in the preceding semester; the President and Administrative Vice-President had to be full-time students, and the Treasurer had to have completed three hours of accounting.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Article II

structure.fact: Under the consolidated text, Congress was composed of the president and vice president of each of the four classes, one Academic Council representative and one alternate from each academic college (Potter, Ogden, Business, Graduate and Education), five on-campus representatives, five off-campus representatives, five representatives-at-large, two freshman representatives elected each fall, and the five executive officers. All but the freshman seats were elected campus-wide in the spring.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Article III, Sections 4-6

structure.fact: The consolidated text lowered the removal threshold. Executive officers and members of Congress could be removed for just cause by a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress on the written endorsement of five members, with no final vote for fourteen days. Judicial Council members required a three-fourths vote, on the endorsement of five members of Congress or five of the Judicial Council. The 1966 requirement that two-thirds of Congress be present for business does not appear in the text.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Articles II, III and IV

structure.fact: Under the consolidated text the Judicial Council had seven regular members and three alternates appointed by the President with a two-thirds vote of Congress, took office within two weeks of the start of the fall term, and had a chairman appointed by the President from the seven rather than elected by the Council. Its powers included judicial review of acts of Congress on the request of a member, the President, the Executive Council or any registered student. The 1986-87 roster names seven members and three alternates, with Dan Woolen as chair.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Article IV; Judicial Council Roster 1986-87

structure.fact: The consolidated text named three constitutional committees: Legislative Research, Rules and Elections, and Student Affairs. The Legislative Research Committee collected and reviewed all proposed legislation after its first reading, determined the constitutionality of legislation and checked it against previous legislation. The amendment sheet bound with the document adds five more standing committees: Delegate, Student Services, Student Rights, Academic Affairs and Public Relations.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Article V and amendment sheet

structure.fact: The consolidated text kept the 1966 amendment rule almost word for word: a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress, then ratification in a referendum by a majority of the student body voting, with all changes subject to University approval. Its ratification article added a third condition, that the constitution took effect at the installation of the officers elected at the next regular election.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, Articles IX and X

structure.fact: The amendment sheet bound with the consolidated constitution is signed by five authors, Lynn Groemling, Daniel Duffy, Kevin Hargrave, Van C. Hodge and Robin Kinman, and sponsored by the Legislative Research, Student Affairs and Student Rights committees. It would have raised the freshman representatives from two to four, added one delegate from every university-recognised organisation, and tied quorum to the number of organisations sending a delegate.
structure.src_label: Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, amendment sheet

structure.fact: The by-laws were rewritten in a run of bills across the period: 89-01-F, 89-02-F and 89-03-F on 5 September 1989 on the President's Board, on legislation and on the order of business; 90-1-F on sponsorship of bills and resolutions; 91-4-S suspending the by-laws, 91-5-S amending how resolutions were submitted, 91-6-S on overriding a presidential veto, and 91-07-F on mandatory legislation.
structure.src_label: SGA legislation index, Bills 89-01-F to 91-07-F

unanswered:
What became of the constitution students ratified on 10 December 1970. The Herald says it was going to the administration and then the Board of Regents; nothing in the archive records either acting on it. Revision work resumed in January and February 1971 and produced a different document sixteen months later, and the Herald of 31 March 1972 calls that one the work of two bodies of Congress. Whether the 1970 text was rejected, withdrawn or simply absorbed is not established.

How the April 1968 treasurer amendment was decided. The ballot survives with its text; Ron Beck's results memo of 3 May 1968 reports every officer race and the 2,894 turnout but is silent on both the amendment and the $1.50 fee question on the same ballot.

The substance of most amendments. The archive holds headlines and not texts for the four changes voted on 1 May 1970, the October 1970 quorum question, the amendment that passed at the fall 1971 freshman election, the amendments on the November 1973 ballot, the constitution amendments passed on 8 February 1979, the revised constitution approved on 30 November 1978, and the 1983 revisions. No copy of any of them was found.

The date the typed 1986 constitution actually reflects. TopSCHOLAR dates the item 4 August 1986, but its Article II, Section 3 makes the ASG President the student member of the Board of Regents, with a special election only if the President is not a Kentucky resident, while the Herald of 3 February 1983 carried President Margaret Ragan explaining that the presidency and the regent seat were then separate. Either the typed base text predates 1983 or the archive's account of the split needs revisiting. The amendment sheet bound with it carries no date at all, and three of its five authors are people the record places in 1988 to 1991.

Whether the 1986 consolidation was ever ratified. Its own Article X required University approval, a majority of students voting, and installation of the next officers. No referendum on it appears in the Herald index.

No by-laws survive for this period. The earliest by-laws in the TopSCHOLAR SGA collection are dated 1994, although the 1966 constitution required that all election laws and regulations live in the by-laws and bills amended them repeatedly from 1986 onward.

Judicial Council membership is documented for two years only, 1976-77 and 1986-87. Nothing in the archive shows when the Council changed from electing its own chairman under the 1966 text to having one appointed by the President as in the consolidated text, or when it gained three alternates; the seven-plus-three structure is already visible in 1976-77.

A large body of material was not worked in this run. TopSCHOLAR holds 843 sets of SGA minutes, of which about 240 fall between 1976 and 1992, including runs of 27 meetings in 1982 and 1983 and 34 in 1989. Those minutes would settle most of the questions above. digitalcommons.wku.edu blocks direct PDF downloads with an AWS WAF challenge; every document read here was retrieved through the Wayback Machine copy of the same file.
